request.user:
[2024 fall ms applied — problem 4]

Multiple regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, X_3$, $n = 25$, SS(Total) $= 248.0$; table of SSReg for all predictor subsets (SSReg($X_1,X_2,X_3) = 181.8$, SSReg($X_1,X_2) = 145.2$, etc.), $\alpha = 0.05$. (1) Global F-test of $H_0: \beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0$. (2) Compute the extra SSReg$(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)$. (3) Test whether $X_3$ can be dropped. (4) Write the first row of the reduced-model $X$-matrix testing $H_0: \beta_2 = \beta_3 = 0$ (first obs: $Y=10, X_1=1985, X_2=59.7, X_3=2205$).

response.text:
**Given:** \(n=25\), \(SS_T=248.0\), and for the full model with predictors \(X_1,X_2,X_3\),

\[
SSReg(X_1,X_2,X_3)=181.8.
\]

Thus

\[
SSE_{\text{full}}=SS_T-SSReg_{\text{full}}
=248.0-181.8=66.2.
\]

The full model has \(p=3\) predictors plus intercept, so

\[
df_E=n-p-1=25-3-1=21.
\]

Therefore

\[
MSE_{\text{full}}=\frac{66.2}{21}=3.1524.
\]

---

## (1) Global \(F\)-test of \(H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0\)

The global test statistic is

\[
F=\frac{MSReg}{MSE}
=\frac{SSReg/p}{SSE/(n-p-1)}.
\]

So

\[
F=\frac{181.8/3}{66.2/21}
=\frac{60.6}{3.1524}
\approx 19.22.
\]

The degrees of freedom are

\[
df_1=3,\qquad df_2=21.
\]

At \(\alpha=0.05\),

\[
F_{0.95;3,21}\approx 3.07.
\]

Since

\[
19.22>3.07,
\]

we reject \(H_0\).

**Conclusion:** The overall regression is significant at the \(0.05\) level. At least one of \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\) is nonzero.

---

## (2) Extra sum of squares \(SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)\)

By definition,

\[
SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)
=
SSReg(X_1,X_2,X_3)-SSReg(X_1,X_2).
\]

Given

\[
SSReg(X_1,X_2,X_3)=181.8,
\qquad
SSReg(X_1,X_2)=145.2,
\]

we get

\[
SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)
=
181.8-145.2
=
36.6.
\]

\[
\boxed{SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)=36.6}
\]

---

## (3) Test whether \(X_3\) can be dropped

We test

\[
H_0:\beta_3=0
\]

given that \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are already in the model.

The test statistic is

\[
F=\frac{SSReg(X_3\mid X_1,X_2)/1}{MSE_{\text{full}}}.
\]

Thus

\[
F=\frac{36.6/1}{66.2/21}
=
\frac{36.6}{3.1524}
\approx 11.61.
\]

The degrees of freedom are

\[
df_1=1,\qquad df_2=21.
\]

At \(\alpha=0.05\),

\[
F_{0.95;1,21}\approx 4.32.
\]

Since

\[
11.61>4.32,
\]

we reject \(H_0\).

**Conclusion:** \(X_3\) provides a significant contribution after accounting for \(X_1\) and \(X_2\). Therefore, \(X_3\) should **not** be dropped from the model.

---

## (4) First row of the reduced-model \(X\)-matrix for testing \(H_0:\beta_2=\beta_3=0\)

The full model is

\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+\beta_3X_3+\varepsilon.
\]

Testing

\[
H_0:\beta_2=\beta_3=0
\]

means the reduced model is

\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\varepsilon.
\]

Therefore the reduced-model design matrix contains only the intercept column and the \(X_1\) column.

For the first observation,

\[
Y=10,\qquad X_1=1985,\qquad X_2=59.7,\qquad X_3=2205.
\]

The first row of the reduced-model \(X\)-matrix is therefore

\[
\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1985\end{bmatrix}}.
\]

The response value \(Y=10\) is not part of the \(X\)-matrix.
